client: Since I lost my job last month, I’ve been constantly worrying about money and my career. I feel stuck and unsure about what to do next, and it’s hard to shake the fear that I’ll never find something stable again. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with something as practical as this, but here I am.
therapist: It sounds like this has been a really challenging time for you, and it’s understandable to feel stuck and uncertain when facing such a significant change. You mentioned feeling unsure about what to do next—can you tell me a bit more about what you’ve tried so far or what steps feel most daunting to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I've updated my resume and applied to a few jobs, but every time I think about networking or reaching out to contacts, I freeze up. It's like my mind goes blank and I convince myself nobody would want to hire someone who got laid off. I know that's probably irrational, but the anxiety feels so real in the moment.
therapist: It sounds like you’re taking some proactive steps, like updating your resume, which is great, but the anxiety around networking seems to be holding you back. When you freeze up, what’s the worst-case scenario that comes to mind? Let’s unpack that thought a bit.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the worst-case scenario is that they’ll judge me or think I’m not good enough because I got laid off. Or maybe they’ll just ignore me completely, and I’ll feel even more rejected and embarrassed. It’s like I’m already assuming the outcome will be negative before I even try, which I know isn’t helpful, but it’s hard to stop thinking that way.
therapist: It sounds like you're really sitting with that fear of judgment, and your voice tells me this feels particularly heavy for you right now. You're already recognizing that these thoughts might be jumping ahead—what do you think is underneath that immediate assumption of rejection? Is there a past experience making this feel especially vulnerable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, actually... my last boss made some comments when they let me go about how the company "needed to move in a different direction." Even though they said it wasn't personal, it really made me question my skills. Now I keep wondering if other employers will see me the same way - like I wasn't good enough to keep around. Logically I know layoffs happen to lots of people, but it still feels personal to me.
therapist: That comment from your boss seems to have really stuck with you—it makes sense that it would leave you questioning your worth, even if intellectually you know layoffs are common. Would it be helpful to explore how we might separate that one painful experience from your actual skills and value as an employee?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I do want to separate those feelings, but part of me worries that if I stop being hard on myself, I'll become complacent or stop trying as hard. The self-doubt kind of fuels me, even though I know it's not healthy. How do people stay motivated without beating themselves up?
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears—that letting go of self-doubt might mean losing your drive, while also recognizing this pattern isn't serving you well. What if motivation could come from a place of self-encouragement rather than self-criticism—what might that look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've never really thought about motivation coming from a positive place before. It feels... almost unnatural, like I wouldn't trust it to be strong enough. But I'm exhausted from the constant self-criticism, so I guess I'm willing to try, though I'm skeptical it'll work for someone like me. How do you even start building that kind of mindset?
therapist: I hear both curiosity and hesitation in your voice—this idea of positive motivation feels unfamiliar and maybe even uncomfortable to trust. Let’s start small: what’s one thing you’ve accomplished in the past that you *could* feel genuinely proud of, even if it feels hard to acknowledge right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: Hmm... I did finish a big certification program while working full-time a few years ago. I guess that was impressive when I think about it, but it's hard not to dismiss it now as just being "in the past." My brain keeps saying "That was then, what have you done lately?" which kind of ruins any good feeling about it.
therapist: It’s interesting—even as you downplay that achievement, there’s a spark in your voice when you mention it. That voice saying "what have you done lately?" is pretty harsh—what would it feel like to talk to yourself about that certification the way you’d talk to a friend who’d accomplished the same thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I tried imagining that just now, and it felt... weirdly uncomfortable. If a friend told me they'd done that, I'd say "That's amazing, balancing work and studying is so hard!" But when I say it to myself, it feels like I'm being arrogant or making excuses. Maybe that's part of why job searching is so hard - I don't trust my own achievements to matter.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real disconnect between how you’d celebrate a friend’s accomplishment and how you allow yourself to acknowledge your own. That discomfort you’re feeling—do you think it might be tied to a belief that self-recognition is somehow arrogant or undeserved? Let’s explore where that belief might come from.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it goes back to my dad always saying "don't toot your own horn" growing up. He made it seem like any kind of self-praise was showing off. But now I realize I've taken that to an extreme where I can't even privately acknowledge my own successes without feeling guilty. It's frustrating because logically I know that's not healthy, but the feeling is still there.
therapist: It sounds like your dad’s message about humility has stayed with you, but it’s evolved into something that’s now holding you back from recognizing your own worth. How do you think your approach to job searching—and even your confidence—might shift if you allowed yourself to "toot your own horn" a little more?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would feel... lighter, maybe? But also kind of scary, like I'd be setting myself up for disappointment if I start believing in my own worth and then don't get the job. It's like I'd rather stay small and not take the risk of putting myself out there confidently. Is that normal?
therapist: It sounds like you’re grappling with a tension between wanting to feel lighter and the fear of disappointment that comes with putting yourself out there. Staying small feels safer, but I wonder if it’s also keeping you from opportunities that could align with your true worth. What would it feel like to take just one small step toward acknowledging your value, even if it feels risky?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
